papers.title: Byzantine-Robust Federated Machine Learning through Adaptive Model Averaging

C-a.quote: We propose an algorithm that aims to detect and discard bad or malicious client’s updates at every iteration by comparing the similarity of these individual updates to the one for the aggregated model. In contrast to other robust federated algorithms, we propose a method to estimate the quality of the client’s updates through a Hidden Markov Model. This allows us to define a mechanism to block faulty, noisy or malicious clients that systematically send bad model updates to the server
C-a.locator: Introduction; the two stages meet in Eq. (3), whose weighted average runs over the filtered subset K_t^g AND weights each surviving client by the HMM posterior p_k^t

C-b.quote: This allows us to define a mechanism to block faulty, noisy or malicious clients that systematically send bad model updates to the server, reducing the communication burden between the clients and the server and the time required by the server to compute the aggregated model
C-b.locator: Introduction; restated in the Abstract as "This includes a mechanism that blocks unwanted participants, which also increases the computational and communication efficiency."

C-c.quote: AFA is robust in all scenarios for the 4 datasets, i.e. the test error of the algorithm is not significantly degraded
C-c.locator: Robustness and Convergence, Table 1

C-d.quote: The results of our experimental evaluation are shown in Table 1. We considered two cases with 10 and 100 clients for the 4 previously described scenarios.
C-d.locator: Robustness and Convergence, Table 1

C-e.quote: We also showed that AFA is very effective at detecting bad clients and capable of blocking them within a reduced number of training iterations.
C-e.locator: Conclusion; the supporting artifact is Table 2, "Percentage of bad clients blocked by AFA and the average number of training iterations to block them"

papers.coder_note:
C-b IS THE CODE THAT DECIDES THIS PAPER, AND IT TURNS ON WHAT THE SECOND STAGE IS FOR. AFA does compose two mechanisms in one round (a cosine-similarity outlier discard against the running aggregate, and a Beta-Bernoulli/HMM client-quality posterior that both weights the survivors and permanently blocks persistent offenders), so C-a is YES. But every reason the paper gives for the second stage is a COST reason, not a coverage or standalone-effectiveness reason: it reduces communication burden, server aggregation time, and the number of clients queried. Nothing says the similarity filter leaves a residue the reputation stage is chosen to cover. The quotation admits a second reading -- "clients that systematically send bad model updates" could be read as a temporal failure mode the per-iteration filter cannot see -- and ambiguity rule 3 takes the reading that makes the paper NOT outcome-gated, so C-b = NO. Primary = NO.

C-d is NO on the strict rubric and on rule 4 both. Table 1 varies the ADVERSARY scenario (clean/byzantine/flipping/noisy) and the COMPETING algorithm (FA, MKRUM, COMED), never AFA's own upstream stage with its downstream held fixed; there is no AFA-minus-HMM or AFA-minus-filter arm anywhere in the paper, appendix included. Table 2 reports the percentage of bad clients blocked, which is the upstream stage's own outcome -- the same thing DeepSight's Table IX does, and the same reason it is not the contrast the rubric asks for. The extractor's single C-d candidate ("This removes the reliance on a pre-specified parameter k ... which would otherwise be discarded in the case of Zeno") is a comparison to a DIFFERENT DEFENSE, not a within-defense variation.

C-e is NO for the same reason C-d is: the conclusion asserts the detector detects well and asserts AFA is robust, but never joins them into a claim that AFA's robustness is BECAUSE of a named stage. The nearest thing is a cross-algorithm contrast ("MKRUM and COMED are very sensitive to label flipping attacks, whereas AFA's performance is barely affected"), which attributes nothing internally.

Note for the shipped table: the extractor's C-a and C-c buckets both returned ZERO candidates on this paper, and both criteria nonetheless code YES off targeted greps. This is the recall limit of the aid, not of the frame -- the paper says "aggregation rule" where the bucket looks for "components", and reports "test error" where the bucket looks for ASR. Two more papers in the frame are pre-2020 and will read the same way.
papers.screen_reason: pipeline: HMM update-quality model, robust aggregation rule and participant blocking (Adaptive Federated Averaging)

papers.title: FLTrust: Byzantine-robust Federated Learning via Trust Bootstrapping

C-a.quote: Therefore, we further clip the cosine similarity score using the popular ReLU operation. The ReLU-clipped cosine similarity is our trust score. Then, FLTrust normalizes each local model update by scaling it to have the same magnitude as the server model update. ... Finally, FLTrust computes the average of the normalized local model updates weighted by their trust scores as the global model update
C-a.locator: Introduction; the paper's own enumeration is at §VI-C: "FLTrust has three key features: a root dataset, using ReLU to clip the cosine similarity scores, and normalizing each local model update."

C-b.quote: However, the cosine similarity alone is insufficient because a local model update, whose cosine similarity score is negative, can still have a negative impact on the aggregated global model update. Therefore, we further clip the cosine similarity score using the popular ReLU operation.
C-b.locator: Introduction; the normalization stage carries its own reason in the same paragraph, "Our normalization limits the impact of malicious local model updates with large magnitudes."

C-c.quote: a CNN global model learnt using FLTrust has a testing error rate of 0.04 under all the evaluated attacks on MNIST-0.1
C-c.locator: Introduction, restating §VI; the composed system's own testing error rate and the Scaling attack's success rate are the reported outcomes throughout §VI

C-d.quote: FLTrust-NoReLU. In this variant, the server does not use ReLU to clip the cosine similarity scores of the local model updates when computing their trust scores. • FLTrust-NoNorm. In this variant, the server does not normalize the local model updates to have the same magnitude as the server model update. • FLTrust-ParNorm. In this variant, the server applies partial normalization, i.e., only normalizes the local model up[dates]
C-d.locator: §VI-C "Comparing different variants of FLTrust", Table IV

C-e.quote: The fact that FLTrust outperforms FLTrust-NoReLU, FLTrust-NoNorm, and FLTrust-ParNorm indicates the necessity of our ReLU operation and normalization.
C-e.locator: §VI-C, read off Table IV

papers.coder_note:
ALL FIVE YES, SO PRIMARY = NO, AND THIS IS THE SECOND HALF OF THE CORRECTION main.tex:1654 NEEDS. That line asserts FLTrust is "proposed and evaluated as a single stage"; the paper names three features of its own accord and evaluates five variants of them in Table IV. Our own prose already knew this: main.tex:906 describes FLTrust as gating "on the scale-invariant cos(u_i, g_srv) and then renormaliz[ing] every update to ||g_srv||", which is two operations, and §VI-C's ParNorm arm is a THIRD level of that same stage.

WHY THIS IS C-d ON THE STRICT READING AND NOT ONLY BY RULE 4. The rubric refuses a leave-one-out that changes the system rather than the upstream input to a fixed component. Here the downstream component -- the trust-score-weighted average -- is bit-for-bit the same in FLTrust, FLTrust-NoNorm and FLTrust-ParNorm, the attack set is held fixed, and the normalization stage feeding it takes three levels (full / partial / none). That is a graded variation of the upstream stage with the downstream mechanism held fixed, the same shape as FLAME's Table 1 (none / clustering / clustering+clipping with the noising fixed), and it is coded the same way for the same reason. FLTrust-NoReLU is a second instance with the roles swapped: the trust-score stage varies while normalization and the weighted average stay fixed.

WHAT IS NOT THE BASIS FOR THE CODE. FLTrust-Server and FLTrust-withServer change WHO contributes an update, not the upstream input to a fixed downstream stage, and the paper's stated reason for their failure is a property of the root dataset ("because the root dataset is small"), not a suppression reading. Neither is counted.

FLTrust was admitted to the frame precisely to decide this claim (see its screen_reason), and it decided it against us. That is the third of three named seeds to code C-d = YES.
papers.screen_reason: borderline, included per the borderline rule: root-dataset trust scoring plus update magnitude normalisation. main.tex:1654 asserts FLTrust is a single stage; coding against full text decides it, which is the point of admitting it (FLTrust)

C-a.locator: §4.3 FLAME Design

C-b.quote: Proposed defenses against backdoor attacks based on detecting and filtering out malicious model updates consider only very specific and limited attacker models, whereas defenses based on differential privacy-inspired noise injection significantly deteriorate the benign performance of the aggregated model.
C-b.locator: Abstract; the complementary-deficiency argument is restated at §4.3 as clustering "to remove poisoned models with large cosine distances" and adaptive clipping "to remove poisoned models with large magnitudes"

C-d.locator: §5.1, Table 1

C-e.quote: As a result, FLAME can use a small Gaussian noise to eliminate the remaining backdoors after applying clustering and clipping, which is beneficial for preserving the main task accuracy.

Table 1 holds the DOWNSTREAM mechanism fixed (Gaussian noising) and varies the UPSTREAM stage across three levels -- none, clustering, clustering+clipping -- reading off the noise scale each level requires. papers.title: BROADCAST: Reducing Both Stochastic and Compression Noise to Robustify Communication-Efficient Federated Learning

C-a.quote: Our work is among the first attempts to jointly consider Byzantine-robust aggregation and compression in federated learning.
C-a.locator: §1 Contributions; the purpose of the compression stage is stated in the Abstract, "Various recent works have proposed to compress the local stochastic gradients to mitigate the communication overhead"

C-b.quote: We theoretically point out that different to the attacks-free compressed stochastic gradient descent (SGD), its vanilla combination with geometric median-based robust aggregation seriously suffers from the compression noise in the presence of Byzantine attacks.
C-b.locator: Abstract

C-c.quote: We present numerical experiments to illustrate the effectiveness of BROADCAST and compare it with existing Byzantine-robust distributed learning algorithms.
C-c.locator: §6 Numerical Experiments, Figure 5 (classification accuracy under no attack, Gaussian, sign-flipping and zero-gradient attacks)

C-d.quote: If δ is 0, meaning that no compression is applied, the learning error in BROADCAST is in the same order as that of the Byzantine-robust SAGA without compression.
C-d.locator: §5.3, after Theorem 2 (Eq. 38-39); the same variation is run in the other direction at §3.3 "Impact of Compression and Stochastic Noise"

C-e.quote: The reason is intuitive: Since even the compressed messages sent from the regular workers are noisy, it is difficult to recognize the malicious ones among them.
C-e.locator: §3.3 Impact of Compression and Stochastic Noise

papers.coder_note:
C-a = NO UNDER AMENDMENT 3: THE SECOND COMPONENT IS COMPRESSION, AND THE PAPER SAYS IT IS FOR COMMUNICATION. Only one component here resists malicious updates (geometric-median aggregation); the compressor exists to cut the communication bottleneck and the variance-reduction step exists to cancel stochastic noise. Neither is a defense by stated purpose. Primary = NO.

THE FINDING IN THIS ROW IS C-d, AND IT IS A ROUTE NEITHER THE PRE-REGISTRATION NOR THE PAPER ANTICIPATED: BROADCAST RUNS THE IDENTIFYING CONTRAST ANALYTICALLY. §3.3 holds the downstream mechanism fixed (geometric-median aggregation), holds the attack fixed (Byzantine workers), varies the upstream stage (compression on, with compression noise delta; compression off), and reads the downstream mechanism's loss of suppression off that variation -- "even with unbiased compressors, the Byzantine-robust compressed SGD still suffers from" the compression noise, and the reason given is that the noise destroys the very signal the median needs to recognize malicious workers. §5.3 then runs the same variation in the other direction on the composed system: set delta = 0 and BROADCAST's learning error returns to the uncompressed Byzantine-robust SAGA's order. The intervention is in the error bound rather than in a table, and the frozen C-d text does not require an experiment -- it requires that the upstream stage be varied with the downstream mechanism and the attack held fixed, which this is. Rule 4's benefit of the doubt would reach the same code if the analytic form were thought insufficient.

This is the third distinct route to C-d in six coded papers, and they are worth naming together because the appendix table will otherwise read as though C-d means one thing: FLAME/FLTrust vary a defense stage in a table; SHARE and zPROBE sweep a hyperparameter of a stage they introduced; BROADCAST varies an upstream stage inside a convergence bound. Only the first was foreseen.

C-e is unambiguous and is a MECHANISM claim in the strict sense -- it says why the composition behaves as it does, in terms of what the upstream stage does to the downstream stage's input. The paper is a counterexample to the sharp reading of our own related-work sentence, and it is a 2021 preprint, i.e. it predates the claim.
papers.screen_reason: pipeline: compression composed with geometric-median robust aggregation, whose vanilla combination the paper analyses (BROADCAST)

papers.title: Secure Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning via Clustering

C-a.quote: To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first approach that scalably combines Byzantine-robustness with privacy using the common single-server architecture.
C-a.locator: Introduction; the purpose of the clustering stage is stated as "These nonlinear operations adversely affect privacy since privacy-preserving methods such as secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) are inefficient for nonlinear operations [3]", and the architecture claim is "we propose a modified federated learning architecture to incorporate any robustness protocol in a privacy preserving manner" (§6)

C-b.quote: Taken together, this manuscript proposes a federated learning architecture that preserves security and privacy jointly, thus addressing this gap in the literature.
C-b.locator: Introduction

C-c.quote: Figure (2a) shows that SHARE with a strong defense like Zeno++ converges to benign (no-attack) accuracy for any of the considered cluster sizes.
C-c.locator: §6.1 CIFAR-10, Figure 2

C-d.quote: Figure 2: Results of SHARE with various defenses on CIFAR-10, utilizing varying cluster sizes under label flip attack.
C-d.locator: §6.1, Figure 2; Figure 3 repeats it for reclustering rounds, "Results of SHARE with Zeno++ and different reclustering rounds R, Byzantine clients q, cluster sizes m on CIFAR-10 with varying attack strengths"

C-e.quote: SHARE with trimmed mean and Krum both converge with cluster size 3 but as cluster size increases, accuracy decreases and SHARE begins to diverge. This can be seen directly from Lemma 2
C-e.locator: §6.1, reading Figure 2 against Lemma 2 ("Algorithm 1 is robust to q = q_0 m adversaries, where q_0 is the tolerance limit of the robust aggregation oracle followed and m is the cluster size")

papers.coder_note:
C-a = NO UNDER AMENDMENT 3, AND THE PAPER'S OWN SENTENCE IS WHY: it combines robustness with PRIVACY, not two defenses. The only component whose stated purpose is resisting malicious updates is the robust aggregation oracle, which SHARE treats as a black box supplied from outside (Krum, trimmed mean, Zeno++ are plugged in interchangeably). Clients are clustered so that secure aggregation can avoid nonlinear operations under MPC; that is a cryptographic feasibility device, and the paper says so. Primary = NO.

BUT C-d = YES ON THE STRICT READING, AND THIS PAPER IS THE CLEANEST NON-SEED INSTANCE SO FAR. Within each panel of Figure 2 the downstream mechanism is fixed (one aggregator per panel: Zeno++, Krum, trimmed mean), the attack is fixed (label flip, q=12), and the ONLY thing varied is the upstream stage's parameter -- cluster size, i.e. how much averaging happens before the aggregator sees anything. The composed system's accuracy is read off that variation, and the reading is then attributed to Lemma 2's q = q_0 m. That is the intervention prop:identification_full describes, run on a privacy stage rather than a defense stage. Figure 3 does the same for reclustering rounds R with Zeno++ held fixed, and Figure 5 repeats the cluster-size sweep across three aggregators under the FoE attack.

The combination -- C-a = NO but C-d = YES -- is worth flagging for the appendix table's prose, because it is the shape a reader will not predict: a paper can run the identifying contrast without composing two defenses at all, and this one runs it because cluster size is a hyperparameter it introduced and therefore had to sweep. That is a second route to C-d, and it is not a route this paper's argument anticipated.
papers.screen_reason: pipeline: secure averaging within randomly clustered clients BEFORE robust-aggregation filtering, a stated two-stage order (SHARE)

C-a.quote: zPROBE comprises two main components, namely, secure aggregation, and robustness establishment.
C-a.locator: §3.1 zPROBE Overview; the purpose of the first component is stated in the Abstract, "The server only learns the final aggregation result, thereby preventing leakage of the users' (private) training data from the individual model updates"

C-b.quote: However, implementing privacy-preserving rank-based statistics, especially median-based, is nontrivial and unscalable in the secure domain, as it requires sorting of all individual updates.
C-b.locator: Abstract; restated at §1 as "By co-designing the robustness defense and cryptographic components of zPROBE, we are able to provide a scalable and low overhead solution for private and robust FL"

C-c.quote: zPROBE is robust against various Byzantine attacks with 0.5 − 2.8% higher accuracy compared to prior work on private and robust FL.
C-c.locator: §1 Contributions; Table 1

C-d.quote: Figure 4: Ablation studies on zPROBE defense performance with varying (a) portion of compromised gradients, (b) attack magnitude, (c) number of clients, and (d) number of user clusters.
C-d.locator: §4.2, Figure 4

C-e.quote: we believe can be attributed to 1) the use of rank-based statistics to establish dynamic thresholds, and 2) the use of all benign gradients in the aggregation, rather than replacing all values with a robust aggregator, e.g., as in KRUM.
C-e.locator: §4.1, discussing Table 1

papers.coder_note:
C-a = NO UNDER AMENDMENT 3, ON THE PAPER'S OWN TWO-COMPONENT ENUMERATION. Of zPROBE's two named components, only "robustness establishment" has resisting malicious updates as its stated purpose; secure aggregation is there to keep the server from seeing individual updates. Primary = NO.

THE BORDERLINE, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. zPROBE's zero-knowledge proofs do resist adversarial behaviour -- they stop a malicious client lying about the masks and quantiles it submitted -- so a reader could argue the ZKP layer is a second defense mechanism and code C-a = YES. Two things decide it NO here. First, what the ZKP defends is PROTOCOL EXECUTION, not the model: a client whose proof verifies can still submit a poisoned gradient, and it is the rank-based check, not the proof, that removes it. Second, ambiguity rule 3 takes the reading that makes the paper not outcome-gated. The argument is close enough that it is written down here so a reader who disagrees can flip this one row and see what it does.

C-d = YES, and panel (d) is why: number of user clusters is an upstream stage zPROBE introduced (clients are clustered so medians can be estimated on aggregates rather than on individuals), swept with the downstream rank-based robustness check and the attack held fixed. Panels (a)-(c) are attack-strength and scale sweeps and would not qualify on their own; rule 4's benefit of the doubt is not needed for (d), but would cover it if the clustering were read as part of the check rather than upstream of it.

C-e is unusually explicit and is worth quoting in the shipped table even though the row is not primary: the attribution names two constituents and contrasts them with a third design (KRUM), on the strength of a table of composed-system accuracies. It is the attributional pattern the paper describes, arrived at without the composition C-a asks for.
papers.screen_reason: pipeline: randomized clustering plus rank-based robustness checks (zPROBE)

papers.title: Defending against the Label-flipping Attack in Federated Learning

C-a.quote: Accordingly, we propose a novel defense that first dynamically extracts those gradients from the peers’ local updates, and then clusters the extracted gradients, analyzes the resulting clusters and filters out potential bad updates before model aggregation.
C-a.locator: Abstract; the same three steps are enumerated at §5 ("First, we start by extracting the gradients connected to the identified potential source and target classes ... Then, we use the k-means [13] method with two clusters ... Once the two clusters are formed, we need to decide which of them contains the potential bad updates")

C-b.quote: In this paper, we deeply investigate the LF attack behavior and find that the contradicting objectives of attackers and honest peers on the source class examples are reflected in the parameter gradients corresponding to the neurons of the source and target classes in the output layer, making those gradients good discriminative features for the attack detection.
C-b.locator: Abstract / §4; the reason given is a FEATURE-SELECTION reason for one detector, and no second mechanism is paired with it

C-c.quote: In addition, we compare our approach with several state-of-the-art defenses and show its superiority at simultaneously delivering low test error, high overall accuracy, high source class accuracy, low attack success rate and stability of the source class accuracy.
C-c.locator: §1 Contributions; §6.1 defines the metrics, including "Attack success rate (ASR)"

C-d.quote: In addition, we compare our approach with several state-of-the-art defenses and show its superiority at simultaneously delivering low test error, high overall accuracy, high source class accuracy, low attack success rate and stability of the source class accuracy.
C-d.locator: §6; the experimental axes are the DATA DISTRIBUTION (iid / non-iid / extreme non-iid), the attacker ratio and the competing defense, never this defense's own upstream stage against a fixed downstream one

C-e.quote: focusing on the gradients of the parameters connected to the neurons of the source and target classes in the output layer is more helpful to defend against the attack
C-e.locator: §1 Contributions, where the paper undertakes to "explain analytically why"; the mechanism argument is at §4, "the relevant neurons' errors will stay large during model training because of the contradicting objectives"

papers.coder_note:
C-a = NO BECAUSE THE THREE STEPS ARE ONE DETECTOR, NOT TWO DEFENSES. Extract-then-cluster-then-score-then-filter is a single filtering mechanism realized in stages: the extraction is a feature choice, the k-means and the inverse-density score are the decision rule of that same filter, and what happens after the filter is plain averaging. C-a's own exclusion list rules out "a single mechanism with hyperparameters", and the settled reading that plain FedAvg is not a defense mechanism decides the rest -- otherwise C-a's "filter-then-aggregate" shape would make every filtering defense in the literature code YES, which would empty the criterion of content. Primary = NO.

What the paper is NOT is also worth recording, because it is the paper this frame was expecting to find and did not: it explicitly contrasts itself with CONTRA, which "integrates FGold [11] with a reputation-based mechanism", i.e. it names a genuine two-defense composition in its related work while proposing a single-mechanism defense itself.

C-d = NO on the strict reading and on rule 4 both. Every experimental axis is external to the defense -- data distribution, attacker ratio, model size, competing defense -- and no arm holds the aggregation fixed while varying the filter, or vice versa. There is no ablation table anywhere in the paper; the extractor's C-d bucket returned zero candidates over 78805 characters, and a targeted grep for ablation language found none either.

C-e = YES all the same, and the pattern is the one the audit is measuring in a weaker form: the attributional claim is about which GRADIENTS carry the signal, defended analytically in §4 rather than by an intervention, and supported empirically only by the composed detector's end metrics. It is an attribution claim resting on a composed-system outcome; it simply is not an attribution about a PAIRING, because there is no pairing.

THE C-b QUOTATION WAS REPAIRED AFTER CODING: the word "parameter" had been dropped from "the parameter gradients corresponding to the neurons of the source and target classes" with no elision marker, and the C-a quotation had a straight apostrophe for "peers’". The replacement is the full sentence from source, which also supplies the finding the pairing rests on. No code moves. See results/literature_audit/quote_repair_log.md.
papers.screen_reason: pipeline: clustering-based detection plus pruning against label flipping

papers.title: MUDGUARD: Taming Malicious Majorities in Federated Learning using Privacy-Preserving Byzantine-Robust Clustering

C-a.quote: Considering the upcoming cryptographic clustering, one needs to compute the signs of gradients sign(ĝit ) ∈ {−1, +1} as SignSGD [6] and then encodes to Boolean representation, which is compatible with binary SS and XOR operations.
C-a.locator: §IV (design); the defensive stage's own purpose is stated in the Introduction, "To thwart attacks from a malicious majority, we develop a method called Model Segmentation, that aggregates together only the updates from within a cluster, sending the corresponding model only to the clients of the corresponding cluster"

C-b.quote: Since the adjusted cosine similarity measures the difference in directions and magnitudes of updates at the same time, we use the pairwise adjusted cosine similarity CosM as a method for extracting features, i.e., CosM and L2 distance, used as the input and the main metric of DBSCAN, respectively.
C-b.locator: §IV-A, Fig. 1

C-c.quote: Meanwhile, the attack success rate is around 0%-5% even under an adaptive attack tailored to MUDGUARD.
C-c.locator: Abstract; §VI evaluation, "quantify its accuracy under untargeted attacks, the Attack Success Rate (ASR) under targeted attacks or under an adaptive attack tailored to MUDGUARD"

C-d.quote: To demonstrate the advantages of MUDGUARD (based on SignSGD), we also compare its robustness with both SignSGD and FedAvg w/o defense.
C-d.locator: §VI, MUDGUARD vs SignSGD vs FedAvg-without-defense

C-e.quote: Although SignSGD is lightweight, it brings a negative impact on the accuracy of clustering. Section V-A provides a detailed analysis of this impact.
C-e.locator: §IV, analysed in §V-A

papers.coder_note:
C-a = NO, AND THIS IS THE HARDEST C-a IN THE FRAME SO FAR. MUDGUARD has three candidate stages: DBSCAN clustering on adjusted cosine similarity, Model Segmentation, and SignSGD. Clustering and Model Segmentation are ONE mechanism, not two -- the clustering is the detector and the segmentation is that same detector's response policy ("aggregates together only the updates from within a cluster"), which is why the paper can say it never needs to decide which cluster is malicious. That leaves SignSGD as the only candidate second mechanism, and the paper's stated reason for adopting it is CRYPTOGRAPHIC: signs are what binary secret sharing and XOR can operate on. Amendment 3 therefore does not count it, and ambiguity rule 3 confirms the direction.

The reading is genuinely two-sided and is recorded so a reader can flip it: the paper also says "SignSGD has the natural capability of defending against scaling attacks [3] since it only takes signs as updates and clips the magnitude", which is a defensive purpose stated in the paper's own voice. A coder who weighted that sentence over the compatibility sentence would code C-a = YES. It would not change the primary verdict, because C-d = YES independently.

C-d = YES ON THE STRICT READING, AND IT IS THE FLAME TABLE 1 SHAPE EXACTLY. Three arms: FedAvg with no defense; SignSGD alone; MUDGUARD, which is the clustering-plus-segmentation stage feeding the same SignSGD. Between the last two the downstream mechanism is identical and the upstream stage is the only thing that moves, with the attack held fixed, and the composed system's robustness is read off the difference.

C-e is the most interesting quotation in this row and it runs the OTHER way from the usual attribution: rather than crediting a stage for the defense's success, the paper charges the downstream choice (SignSGD) with degrading the upstream stage's accuracy, and devotes §V-A to analysing that interaction. Exactly one component here has resisting malicious updates as its stated purpose -- the momentum-based clipping of the BREM estimator. The Gaussian noise is there for differential privacy, and the secure-aggregation layer of DP-BREM+ is there so the same privacy holds without a trusted server. THE BORDERLINE, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN, AND IT IS CLOSER HERE THAN IN ANY PRIOR ROW. A reader could code C-a = YES on the pair (client momentum, clipping): both are inside BREM, both are applied to the same round in sequence, and the paper states a ROBUSTNESS purpose for each -- "LFH achieves robustness via client momentum with the motivation of averaging the updates of each client over time, thus reducing the variance of the honest clients and exposing the small malicious perturbations of Byzantine clients that are undetectable in a single round but accumulate over time" (§3.1), while the clipping bounds each client's deviation. Under Amendment 3's purpose test both legs pass, so the question is only whether they are TWO mechanisms or one published aggregation rule. C-e IS THE STRONGEST ATTRIBUTION QUOTATION IN THE FRAME SO FAR, AND IT IS OUR OWN ATTENUATION CHANNEL WRITTEN OUT FOR DP NOISE. Eighteen papers are now coded and this is the first row with the outcome-gated design and no identifying contrast anywhere in the paper. It is therefore the single most consequential row in the audit, and the C-d = NO was decided by reading §V end to end rather than by a bucket count.

WHY C-d = NO SURVIVES BOTH THE STRICT READING AND RULE 4. Section V is two subsections and that is the whole evaluation. §V-A compares AER across FedCC (K-means), FLAME (HDBSCAN) and Fedward (AutoOPTICS); §V-B compares AASR and MA against five baselines. Every axis is external to the defense -- dataset, PDR, NIR, competing system -- and the paper's own framing of §V-A is a MENU ("we conduct experiments for FBA in clustering defense on FedCC (K-means), FLAME (HDBSCAN), and our Fedward (AutoOPTICS), respectively"), which C-a's and C-d's exclusion lists both name. The comparison looks superficially like a clustering-stage contrast, and it is not one: the three clusterers sit inside three different systems, so FedCC and FLAME differ from Fedward in their clipping and noising stages as well, and nothing downstream is held fixed. There is no ablation table, no variant of Fedward with a stage removed or substituted, and no sweep of the clipping bound, the sparsification, or AutoOPTICS's eps. Rule 4's benefit of the doubt has nothing to attach to: there is no experiment that PLAUSIBLY holds a downstream mechanism fixed while varying an upstream stage, because there is no experiment that varies an internal stage at all. The extractor's C-d bucket returned 2 candidates over 32346 characters and neither is a contrast (one is a definition of the ALA attack, one is a line reference in Algorithm 2); a targeted grep for ablation / w/o / impact-of / effect-of language returned four hits, all of them descriptions of attacks or of prior work.

WHY C-a = YES, AND WHY AMENDMENT 3 IS WHAT MAKES THE ROW CORRECT RATHER THAN LUCKY. The middle component is called SPARSIFICATION, and the pre-registration's own reasoning in Amendment 3 says compression is essentially never a defense. Read by the operation's name this row would code C-a = NO and the frame would have lost its only primary. Amendment 3 forbids that reading and requires the purpose be quoted: §IV-B states the purpose as exposing what the downstream filter would otherwise miss -- "The prior studies lack an effective approach to limit AMSA ... Due to the stealthiness of AMSA, our Fedward adopts gradient sparsification to extract the major local model update and then amplifies the major update" -- and §I states it as "which can endeavor to magnify malicious model updates". AmGrad sparsifies in order to AMPLIFY the malicious signal for the clustering stage, which is the opposite of a communication device and is a defense by the amendment's test. This is the first row where Amendment 3 raises a code rather than lowering it, which is worth reporting in A5 because the amendment was written with only its lowering direction disclosed.

C-e IS THE WEAKEST OF THE FOUR CODES AND IS STILL YES. The attributional claims are (i) component-level and cross-system -- Fedward's AER advantage attributed to AutoOPTICS against FedCC's K-means and FLAME's HDBSCAN, and FLAME's instability attributed to "the weak constraint of HDBSCAN" -- and (ii) framework-level in §VI, attributing complete eradication to the AmGrad-plus-AutoOPTICS combination. Both are read off composed-system outcomes with no intervention isolating either constituent, which is exactly the pattern the audit is measuring. papers.coder_note:
THIS ROW WAS A CANDIDATE FOURTH PRIMARY AND I CHECKED IT AS HARD AS DROP, BECAUSE THE HARD NEGATIVE SEARCH IS GENUINELY CLEAN: the paper contains NO component-level arm of any kind. Three independent probes returned zero hits each -- no "w/o" or "without" applied to the normalization, the filter, the ReLU clipping, the scoring or the reference selection; no occurrence of "ablation", "variant", "component-wise" or "each module"; no "only using", "remove the" or "disable". Every table in the paper is either a comparison against external baselines or a sweep of an environment parameter. So if C-d turned on component contrasts alone, FLTG would be the frame's fourth primary and the strongest of them in one respect, since it composes two mechanisms with a real stated reason and never once takes the composition apart.

WHAT DEFEATS THE PRIMARY IS THE ROOT-DATASET-BIAS SWEEP, AND THE DECIDING QUESTION IS WHETHER THE ROOT DATASET IS PART OF THE DEFENSE OR PART OF THE ENVIRONMENT. I coded it as part of the defense, and the paper is explicit: Sec. 3.3 introduces the root dataset as a component of ITS OWN system model, Algorithm 1 lists it among the protocol's requirements, and the server's training on it is a numbered step whose output is the trusted reference the filter needs. That is not a property of the deployment -- an FL operator running FedAvg has no root dataset -- it is a stage the defense adds. The contrast is therefore the same object DDFed's epsilon sweep was: vary what feeds the detector, hold the detector fixed, report the outcome. Contrast with the sweeps I DECLINE as environment: the non-IID degree q, the malicious client fraction, and DROP's grid over client learning rate, batch size and epochs, none of which is a stage the defense introduces.

THE COUNTERFACTUAL, STATED PLAINLY SO A READER CAN OVERTURN THE PRIMARY COUNT. If a reader holds that a data resource is not a "stage", then FLTG's C-d = NO and the primary rate rises from 3 to 4 out of the DESIGN set. That is the single most consequential judgment call in the audit so far, and it is why the full negative search is recorded above rather than summarized. My reason for the coding I chose is that C-d exists to detect whether a paper ever measures a downstream mechanism as a function of its input, and this paper does exactly that six times over -- it simply calls the result a tolerance property rather than an identification.

AND THAT MISLABELLING IS FINDING E'S SIXTH AND CLEAREST INSTANCE. The paper presents the sweep as evidence of ROBUSTNESS TO a nuisance ("tolerance to root dataset bias"), not as evidence about WHAT ITS FILTER DOES to differently-conditioned input, and it draws no constituent-level conclusion from the shape of the response. So the identifying contrast is present in the data and absent from the paper's reasoning, which is precisely the gap Prop. prop:identification_full describes. A4 and A5 should note that the audit's C-d rate therefore OVERSTATES how often the field actually reasons from an identifying contrast; the rate counts the experiment, not the inference. That is a limitation of the primary quantity and it must be disclosed as one rather than being converted into a stronger claim.

C-a = NO IS THE DECIDING CODE AND IT HAS TWO INDEPENDENT ROUTES, WHICH IS WHY THIS ROW IS NOT A CLOSE CALL. Route two is Amendment 3: the paper's OTHER innovation, multi-update averaging, is purposed for stability and non-IID performance rather than for resisting poisoned updates, so even a reader who counts the median filter as a mechanism cannot reach two without inferring a purpose the paper does not state. A5 can cite this row as the case where Amendment 3 and the structural test agree, in contrast to LASA and RKD where the amendment overturned the name-based reading.

THE TITLE IS A FALSE SIGNAL AND IT BELONGS IN A5's LIST OF THEM. The paper is titled "Secure and Private Federated Learning", but there is no privacy mechanism in it: all eleven privacy hits are either FL's baseline no-raw-data property, a promise in the abstract ("designed to enhance both the resilience and privacy guarantees of FL systems"), or descriptions of OTHER people's homomorphic-encryption work in the related section. The GMM joint-decoding stage is not merely arithmetic repair: it performs its own statistical discrimination, "isolates adversarial indices by statistically separating them from noiseaffected but honest evaluations" (Sec. III), and emits a per-user adversarial frequency profile. A reader could reasonably call that a detector, in which case FORTA composes two detectors -- code-domain error localization and distance-based selection -- and C-a = YES. Amendment 3 still gives the right answer -- the substrate's stated purpose is privacy, so it does not count toward two -- but A5 should note this as a third configuration of the privacy class, after DDFed's separable stages and ArKrum's title-only privacy.

papers.coder_note:
THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ROW THE AUDIT HAS PRODUCED FOR THE PAPER'S OWN ARGUMENT, AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS. SpectralKrum is a composed defense whose paper (i) states in advance that its experiments will test whether the composition beats its components AND under what conditions it does not, (ii) reports the composition beside each constituent in isolation across seven attacks, and (iii) concludes with a SCOPE CONDITION rather than a superiority claim: "spectral defenses help when attacks introduce orthogonal variance but provide no advantage when malicious gradients lie within the benign subspace." That is, in substance, the procedure Prop. prop:identification_full asks for and the reporting discipline Sec. 14 asks for, arrived at independently. A4 must not imply that no one in the literature does this. What the audit measures is the RATE, and this row is a NO for the primary quantity precisely because the paper runs the contrast.

IT ALSO SUPPLIES THE FRAME'S THIRD EXTERNAL ANCHOR ON COMPOSITION, AND THE THREE NOW POINT IN THREE DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS -- which is a better citation set than three agreeing ones. Fed-DPRoC (2508.12978) PROVES a robust aggregator's guarantee survives an upstream transform. GuardFed (2511.09294) MEASURES a two-defense hybrid failing to inherit either constituent's protection. SpectralKrum MEASURES a composition whose benefit over its constituents is real in one attack regime and absent in another, and then names the property of the attack that decides which. A3 and A5 should cite all three; together they establish that the composition question is live in the literature, that it has been answered both ways, and that nobody has isolated the mechanism-level dependence the paper's screen isolates.

THE PAPER'S OWN LIMITATIONS SECTION CONTAINS THE ASSUMPTION OUR PAPER NAMES, IN ONE WORD. Proposing a spectral-plus-median hybrid, it writes: "Hybrid Spectral-Median Aggregation.: Coordinatewise statistics (Trimmed Mean, Geometric Median) outperform spectral filters on label-flip and min-max. A hybrid combining spectral projection with coordinate-wise median may inherit complementary strengths." INHERIT is exactly the composition-invariance assumption -- that a composed system acquires its constituents' strengths -- and it is written as a conjecture about a pair the paper did not test, one page after the paper measured that a different pair's benefit is regime-dependent. This is the single best quotation the audit has found for A3, because it is a careful paper, aware of the issue, using the assumption anyway.

C-d = YES, AND THE IMPERFECTION IS REAL AND RECORDED RATHER THAN GLOSSED. Relative to FullKrum, SpectralKrum adds an upstream projection AND a downstream guard, so Table II's Krum-versus-SpectralKrum comparison is a two-variable change, not the single upstream substitution FedSAC's random-clustering arm provided. Rule 4 forgives it -- the Krum selection rule is held fixed as a mechanism and its input representation is what varies -- and a reader who declines rule 4 here would code C-d = NO and make this a FIFTH PRIMARY. I record that counterfactual explicitly because it is the second row (after HRA) where rule 4 alone stands between a paper and the primary count, and A5 must report how much of the measured rate rests on that one ambiguity rule.

THE HYPERPARAMETER ROUTE IS DECLARED UNAVAILABLE HERE, WHICH SETTLES A LINE THE FRAME HAS BEEN APPROACHING SINCE DP2Guard. This paper has a section titled Hyperparameter Analysis listing r, B, trim fraction and q with recommended values and directional reasoning -- and no measured outcome for any setting. A declared range with an explanation is not an identifying contrast; a table of outcomes at several settings is. DP2Guard's beta was the previous closest case and it did report outcomes. A5's stratification by c_d_route must say that the route requires REPORTED RESULTS AT MORE THAN ONE SETTING, or the route degenerates into any paper that names a knob.

SCALE AND HONESTY NOTES, RECORDED BECAUSE THEY BEAR ON HOW MUCH WEIGHT THE ROW CAN CARRY. The evaluation is CIFAR-10 + TinyCNN only, n = 10 sampled from 100, f <= 3, and the paper says so itself in its limitations. Its own headline is a negative-leaning characterization ("Rather than claiming universal superiority"), and Table II shows SpectralKrum's Grand Total below GeometricMedian's and DnC-PMF's. So this is not a paper claiming a strong composition win; it is a paper reporting a conditional one. That makes it better evidence for the audit, not worse, since C-b/C-c/C-d/C-e are about the DESIGN and the CONTRAST, not about the result's sign.

EXTRACTOR NOTE: the aid was at its worst on this paper. C-c returned ONE candidate and it was the qualitative backdoor sentence, not the metric definition. C-d returned TWO candidates, both irrelevant (a related-work sentence about CoordMedian and a sentence about model dimension) -- the THIRTEENTH C-d shortfall, and the framing that defeated it is a sixth distinct one: the contrast is announced in a positioning paragraph and executed in a baseline table, with no ablation vocabulary anywhere (0 hits for "ablation"). C-e returned ZERO candidates. Three of the five coded quotations came from targeted reads of Sections VI-VIII.

papers.title: Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning Framework with Post-Quantum Secure Aggregation for Real-Time Threat Intelligence Sharing in Critical IoT Infrastructure

C-a.quote: To defend against Byzantine attacks while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for IoT environments, we propose an adaptive reputation-based aggregation mechanism that combines multi-metric anomaly detection with dynamic client weighting.
C-a.locator: §3.3; PURPOSE QUOTATIONS FOR EVERY COMPONENT, as non-negotiable 12 requires of this paper's privacy class, and AMENDMENT 3 DECIDES THE COUNT HERE. COUNTED: (1) the reputation-weighted aggregation, whose purpose is stated at §3.3.2, "This aggregation rule down-weights updates from clients with low reputation scores, effectively reducing the influence of suspected Byzantine participants without explicitly excluding them."; (2) the adaptive gradient clipping, a separate stage with its own stated defense purpose at §3.3.2, "To further enhance robustness, we implement gradient clipping on individual client updates before aggregation"; (3) the coordinate-wise trimmed mean that supplies the reference direction for the per-round score, "The trimmed mean provides robustness against outliers while maintaining computational efficiency compared to median-based approaches [49].". EXCLUDED as privacy-purposed: the differential privacy stage, "we integrate differential privacy into the framework by adding calibrated Gaussian noise to client updates before secure aggregation.", and the post-quantum secure aggregation protocol, "To provide cryptographic confidentiality for client updates against quantum adversaries, we design a secure aggregation protocol based on CRYSTALS-Kyber key encapsulation and additively homomorphic encryption.". ALSO EXCLUDED, and this is a new kind of exclusion for the frame: the stratified client selection strategy of §3.3.3 SELECTS ON THE DEFENSE'S OWN REPUTATION SCORE and is therefore defense-shaped, but the only purpose the paper states for it is efficiency and convergence, "To optimize communication efficiency and model convergence, we implement a stratified client selection strategy". C-a reaches YES on the counted three and would reach YES on the reputation weighting and the clipping alone

C-b.quote: To further enhance robustness, we implement gradient clipping on individual client updates before aggregation ... This adaptive clipping prevents extremely large updates from dominating the aggregation even if they originate from high-reputation clients, providing defense-in-depth against sophisticated attacks [50].
C-b.locator: §3.3.2; the elision skips displayed equation (7) and the adaptive threshold C = 2.0 · median, which pdftotext renders out of order. THE REASON FOR PAIRING NAMES THE FIRST CONSTITUENT'S OWN FAILURE MODE: reputation weighting cannot stop a large update from a client whose reputation is high, and the clipping stage is added for that residue -- "even if they originate from high-reputation clients". Two further constituent-property reasons are stated: the magnitude metric is selected for a threat form, "Byzantine attacks often manifest as either abnormally large or small update magnitudes relative to honest participants.", with the composed effect stated at §3.3.1, "This formulation penalizes clients with abnormal update magnitudes while rewarding those with high similarity to the trimmed aggregate."; and the trimmed mean is selected for standalone effectiveness plus cost, quoted in the C-a locator. A fourth, residual-coverage reason for the cross-round memory is at §4.6, "However, the exponential moving average formulation with 𝛾 = 0.9prevents rapid reputation restoration, ensuring that clients with malicious history remain down-weighted even during temporary honest behavior." (the missing space in "0.9prevents" is the extractor's and is preserved, not repaired)

C-c.quote: The framework demonstrates robust performance across all attack strategies, with accuracy degradation limited to 2.5% in the worst case (label flipping attacks).
C-c.locator: §4.3 and "Table 2: Framework Resilience Against Different Byzantine Attack Strategies (30% Byzantine Clients)"; the metric is the ASSEMBLED framework's ROBUST ACCURACY, i.e. accuracy and F1 measured while Byzantine clients attack, reported two ways: against attack strategy at a fixed 30% attacker fraction (Table 2 over "We evaluate four attack types: gradient flipping (negating updates), sign flipping (flipping update signs without magnitude change), label flipping (poisoning local training data), and Gaussian noise injection (adding random noise to updates).") and against attacker fraction ("Figure 1 illustrates the framework's resilience against varying percentages of Byzantine attackers conducting gradient flipping attacks, where malicious clients submit negated model updates."). NO ASR, backdoor-accuracy or attack-success number appears anywhere: the eight hits for ASR/attack-success/backdoor vocabulary over 90163 characters are threat-model prose and bibliography entries. The threat model DECLARES backdoors, "(3) backdoor attacks that embed triggers causing targeted misclassification", and §4 never measures one, so C-c is satisfied on the robust-accuracy branch only

C-d.quote: The experiments were conducted on the NSLKDD dataset with Byzantine fractions ranging from 0% to 40% in increments of 5%.
C-d.locator: §4.3; this is the paper's NEAREST MISS and it fails on the criterion's own words, which require the ATTACK to be held fixed -- the swept quantity is the Byzantine fraction, i.e. the attack, over nine settings. THE ENUMERATION IS COMPLETE: the paper contains exactly four figures and four tables and none is an upstream-vs-fixed-downstream contrast. Table 1 compares four different SYSTEMS with no attacker present, "All methods were evaluated under benign conditions without Byzantine attackers to assess the impact of security mechanisms on model utility."; Table 2 varies the attack type; Figure 2 and Table 3 are overhead breakdowns; Figure 3 varies the CLIENT COUNT and reports latency and memory, "Figure 3 demonstrates the framework's scalability characteristics by measuring aggregation latency and memory consumption as the number of participating clients increases from 10 to 200."; Figure 4 is a single-configuration reputation trajectory; Table 4 compares whole systems, "Table 4 presents a comprehensive comparison of our framework against recently published Byzantine-robust federated learning methods evaluated on the NSL-KDD dataset under 30% Byzantine attackers conducting gradient flipping attacks.". "ablation" has 0 hits; there is no w/o arm, no removed stage, no substituted stage. The hyperparameter route is unavailable because every defense knob is reported at ONE setting only -- γ = 0.9, α = 0.2, τ_high = 3.0, τ_low = 0.1, C = 2.0 · median, k_top = 0.7 -- and the DP budget likewise, "We set 𝜖 = 2.0 and 𝛿 = 10 to provide reasonable privacy protection while limiting accuracy degradation.", with the only statement about other budgets being a possibility rather than a measurement, "Tighter privacy budgets could be achieved by increasing noise magnitude, though this would degrade accuracy beyond acceptable thresholds for operational threat detection systems.". The analytic route is unavailable too: Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Corollary and "convergence analysis" each return 0 hits

C-e.quote: The superior resilience of our framework stems from the adaptive reputation mechanism that progressively identifies malicious participants across multiple rounds, whereas single-round aggregation methods like FedMedian and Krum cannot leverage historical behavior patterns.
C-e.locator: §4.2; the claim names one constituent and says what it contributes to the composed result, contrasted against the single-mechanism family. Restated at §5.1, "This enhanced resilience arises from the multi-round reputation tracking mechanism that leverages temporal consistency patterns unavailable to single-round aggregation methods.", and at §4.6, "The clear separation between honest and Byzantine reputation scores validates the effectiveness of the multi-metric anomaly detection approach combining cosine similarity and magnitude analysis.". THE STRONGEST ATTRIBUTIONAL CLAIM IN THE PAPER IS A CROSS-COMPONENT ONE, at §5.1: "This result stems from the synergistic design where reputation-based aggregation actually filters noisy or low-quality updates that might otherwise degrade model performance, partially compensating for the noise introduced by differential privacy mechanisms."

papers.coder_note:
THIS IS THE FRAME'S FIFTH PRIMARY = YES, AND IT CARRIES THE CLEANEST UNMEASURED CROSS-COMPONENT CLAIM THE AUDIT HAS FOUND. The other four are Fedward (2307.00356), BRFL (2310.13403), DROP (2502.07011) and DP2Guard. What makes this row valuable beyond the count is §5.1's explanation of why the composed system loses almost no accuracy: "reputation-based aggregation actually filters noisy or low-quality updates that might otherwise degrade model performance, partially compensating for the noise introduced by differential privacy mechanisms." That is a claim about how one stage's output changes another stage's contribution -- exactly the quantity Prop. prop:identification_full says requires an intervention -- and the paper has NO ablation (0 hits for "ablation"), NO privacy-budget sweep (ε fixed at 2.0), and NO theory (0 hits for Theorem/Lemma/Proposition/convergence analysis). The compensation is inferred from a single accuracy column. A3 should quote it beside SpectralKrum's "may inherit complementary strengths": SpectralKrum states the inheritance assumption and then tests a version of it, this paper states an interaction as an established finding and never varies either side of it.

THE C-d = NO WAS ESTABLISHED BY COMPLETE ENUMERATION, NOT BY A NEGATIVE GREP, BECAUSE IT DECIDES A PRIMARY. The paper has exactly four figures and four tables; every caption is quoted or paraphrased in the C-d locator and each is accounted for. The nearest miss is Figure 1's Byzantine-fraction sweep, which is a nine-level dose ladder read off the composed system's accuracy -- structurally the right shape, wrong varied quantity: C-d requires the attack held fixed, and the attacker fraction IS the attack. Figure 3's client-count sweep is the second-nearest and fails twice over, since client count is not a stage of the defense and the reported outcomes are latency and memory. Rule 4's benefit of the doubt has nothing to attach to: there is no experiment that plausibly holds a downstream mechanism fixed while varying an upstream stage, in any direction.

AMENDMENT 3 EXCLUDES A COMPONENT THAT IS DOWNSTREAM OF THE DEFENSE'S OWN SIGNAL, WHICH IS A FIFTH DIRECTION FOR THE AMENDMENT AND A5 MUST RECORD IT. §3.3.3's stratified client selection picks the top 70% by REPUTATION -- the very score the Byzantine machinery computes -- and so a coder reading the operation would call it part of the defense. The amendment forbids that inference and demands the stated purpose, and the stated purpose is "To optimize communication efficiency and model convergence", with the supporting sentence about letting new or recovered clients rebuild reputation. So the amendment can exclude a component that consumes the defense's output, not merely one whose name misleads. The count does not depend on it, and the exclusion is recorded because it is the kind of case a reader will test the amendment against.

THE COUNTED PAIR IS REPUTATION WEIGHTING PLUS ADAPTIVE CLIPPING, AND THAT CHOICE MATTERS. The paper's own headline phrase is "combines multi-metric anomaly detection with dynamic client weighting", but the weighting is the APPLICATION of the detection score rather than a second mechanism, and resting C-a on that phrase alone would be the weaker reading. §3.3.2's clipping stage removes the difficulty: it is a distinct operation, applied to the same round, with its own quoted defense purpose, and the trimmed mean is a third. So C-a survives the strictest reading of what counts as two mechanisms.

C-b IS THE RESIDUAL-COVERAGE KIND (RKD's kind), AND ITS QUOTATION IS THE SHARPEST INSTANCE IN THE FRAME. "prevents extremely large updates from dominating the aggregation EVEN IF THEY ORIGINATE FROM HIGH-REPUTATION CLIENTS" names the constituent, names the state in which that constituent fails, and gives that failure as the reason the second stage exists -- in the design section, not retrospectively in results. No rule-3 ambiguity arises. The pairing-reason taxonomy is unchanged at five admissible kinds; this row adds an instance, not a kind.

EXTRACTOR NOTE: the C-c bucket returned ZERO candidates over 90163 characters -- the TWELFTH such failure -- and for the now-familiar reason, that the outcome is accuracy and F1 under untargeted Byzantine attack with no ASR vocabulary. The C-d bucket's candidates were the Byzantine-fraction and client-count sweeps, i.e. it surfaced the two nearest misses and nothing else, which is the FOURTEENTH C-d shortfall. Both the coded C-b and the coded C-a came from reading §3.3 straight through; a coder trusting the aid would have missed the clipping stage entirely and, with it, both codes.

DATA-QUALITY OBSERVATION, RECORDED AND DECIDING NOTHING (the HRA precedent). Every reported number in Tables 1-4 is a single value with no dispersion, no seed count and no confidence interval, and the accuracies cluster in a 1.5-point band across four systems and five attack conditions. The paper also reports a 94%+ accuracy at a 40% Byzantine fraction and remarks that this exceeds "the theoretical 33% Byzantine fault tolerance bound commonly cited in distributed systems literature" without reconciling the two. The frozen screen includes papers on what they propose and evaluate, not on how well; the codes above rest on stated purposes, stated pairing reasons and the presence or absence of experiments, none of which turns on the numbers' precision. §5.5 does disclose the adaptive-attack limitation squarely: "An adversary with knowledge that reputation scores use cosine similarity and magnitude metrics could construct poisoned updates that maintain high similarity to honest updates while still degrading model performance through subtle manipulations [74]."

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Averaging with Byzantine Aggregators in Asynchronous Networks

C-a.quote: To address this issue, we use a PVAHSS scheme. This mechanism enables the verification of the intra- and inter-cluster aggregates (or sums), ensuring that each aggregate is consistent with the committed values. The verifications are performed by the aggregators themselves at the end of each round. ... Byzantine processes can voluntarily bias their client inclusion by including in priority some clients rather than others, thereby biasing their own models due to data heterogeneity, but also biasing others aggregators’ models in the inter-cluster aggregation phase. To solve this problem, we add a fraud detection mechanism.
C-a.locator: §6 and §C.1; AMENDMENT 3 DOES ALMOST ALL THE WORK ON THIS ROW, because the paper's own headline composition is entirely privacy-purposed: "Our design combines several key mechanisms: clustering clients under verifiable coordinators, lightweight LWE-based masking (with masking components distributed across aggregators), and differential privacy applied to both intermediary and final aggregated models." -- clustering, LWE masking and DP, all three excluded. The clustering's stated purpose is communication scale, "This design significantly reduces communication overhead with a potentially large number of clients, while SS ensures that an individual gradient 𝑔𝑖𝜏 + 𝑒𝑖 is never reconstructed by Byzantine aggregators without the participation of 𝑛𝑎 − 2𝑡𝑎 > 𝑡𝑎 + 1 correct aggregators."; the quorum threshold's stated purpose is privacy, "To cope with this adversarial setting, we require that 𝑛𝑎 > 3𝑡𝑎 . This threshold ensures protection from equivocation of Byzantine processes, thus enforcing the client[']s privacy"; and the inclusion mechanism's stated purpose is DEBIASING PARTICIPATION, not resisting bad updates, "Such bias is introduced when aggregators include fast clients first due to asynchronous communications and heterogeneous data. To solve this problem, we introduce a “debiasing” client inclusion mechanism.". WHAT SURVIVES THE AMENDMENT IS TWO MECHANISMS AIMED AT A MISBEHAVING AGGREGATOR: the PVAHSS aggregate verification (quoted above, whose commitment leg is stated at §6 as "to ensure that no aggregator misbehave by sending a wrong sum of client['s shares]") and the inclusion fraud detection (quoted above). Both run in every round -- the PVAHSS verifications "are performed by the aggregators themselves at the end of each round", and Algorithm 2 lines 24-29 run the inclusion check each round -- so they are applied jointly to the same round. THE SCOPE CAVEAT THAT A READER MUST WEIGH IS RECORDED HERE AND NOT BURIED: the thing resisted is a Byzantine AGGREGATOR, never a poisoning client. The paper's clients are not adversarial at all, "We consider a set of 𝑛𝑐 honest-butcurious clients, among which up to 𝑡𝑐 may crash. Crashed clients stop participating indefinitely but never behave maliciously.", and the paper's own taxonomy names the excluded class, "When adversaries target the model by submitting syntactically well-formed updates that nevertheless sabotage convergence, e.g., poisoned gradients or models, we call them model-Byzantine adversaries.", and places itself outside it for clients, "Unlike our solution, that tolerates only honest-but-curious clients, this mechanism can tolerate integrity-Byzantine clients, up to n - 2". C-a = YES therefore reads Amendment 3's "faulty, malicious or poisoned updates" as covering a wrong aggregation share and a maliciously biased cluster aggregate, which are updates entering the composition from a Byzantine participant

C-b.quote: Edge cases. The inclusion mechanism can induce two specific edge cases. First, a Byzantine aggregator could decide to bias its clients selection by not using the inclusion algorithm. We propose to use an inclusion fraud detection mechanism to alleviate any such Byzantine misbehaviour.
C-b.locator: §C.1; THIS QUOTATION IS THE PAPER'S ONLY REASON FOR PAIRING AND IT PAIRS A COUNTED MECHANISM WITH AN EXCLUDED ONE. The fraud detector is added because the INCLUSION MECHANISM creates the attack surface it closes -- a real constituent-property reason, of the residual-coverage kind -- but Amendment 3 excises the inclusion mechanism from C-a's count as fairness-purposed, so the reason does not justify the pairing C-a actually certifies (PVAHSS verification with fraud detection). No quotation gives a reason for pairing those two: each is introduced separately against a distinct protocol failure mode ("To address this issue, we use a PVAHSS scheme" for unverifiable aggregates; "To solve this problem, we add a fraud detection mechanism" for biased inclusion), which is composition by requirement rather than by constituent property. Rule 3 points the same way. Targeted searches for pairing language returned only cost and tractability reasons attached to the PRIVACY components -- masking chosen over homomorphic encryption on cost, the single-coordinator design chosen to avoid running a BFT consensus protocol -- which are the taxonomy's inadmissible mathematical-convenience kind, and "complementary" occurs twice, once about RDP noise composition and once about the two aspects evaluated in §7.2

C-c.quote: In Figure 15, we show the difference between an execution with this type of Byzantine behaviour with and without the inclusion fraud detection mechanism both on the MNIST and CIFAR-5m dataset. ... The main impact of such Byzantine behaviour on the accuracy is visible as, without the fraud detection mechanism, accuracy lines are way more jagged than its fraud detection counterpart. This is due to the fact that the Byzantine aggregator draws everyone down.
C-c.locator: §D.5 with "Figure 15: Impact of aggregator’s Byzantine behaviour on the accuracy without the fraud detection mechanism (left) and with the fraud detection mechanism (right). Results on the MNIST dataset (top) and the CIFAR-5m dataset (bottom)."; the metric is the assembled protocol's ROBUST ACCURACY -- accuracy trajectories while a Byzantine aggregator actively biases its client inclusion, "To do so, we simulated a Byzantine behaviour, where an aggregator voluntarily bias its included clients to include in priority fastest clients." -- on two datasets. ASR, attack-success and backdoor vocabulary return 0 hits each over 129438 characters, so the C-c bucket returned ZERO candidates, the THIRTEENTH such failure. TWO CAVEATS RECORDED: the composed system evaluated in these arms has DP DISABLED ("We tested this setup by letting 𝑡𝑎 aggregators simulate a crash after round 10 with the MNIST dataset in a similar setting as the geodistributed setting presented in Section 7, with 𝑛𝑐 = 1500, 𝑟ℎ𝑜 = 128, 𝑡𝑐 = 374, and no differential privacy." for the companion crash experiment, and "All experiments use 𝑛𝑐 = 1500 clients and a single aggregator (𝑡𝑎 = 0, 𝜌 = 128), without DP." for the inclusion arms), so what is validated is the counted defense pair inside the protocol rather than the full stack; and the reported effect is the SMOOTHNESS of the accuracy curve, with the hedge quoted under C-e denying a clear effect on maximum accuracy

C-d.quote: Figure 15: Impact of aggregator’s Byzantine behaviour on the accuracy without the fraud detection mechanism (left) and with the fraud detection mechanism (right). Results on the MNIST dataset (top) and the CIFAR-5m dataset (bottom).
C-d.locator: §D.5, Figure 15; the fraud detector is present in one arm and absent in the other with the Byzantine behaviour, the datasets, the assignment and the aggregation all held fixed, and the outcome read off the composed system's accuracy. THE DIRECTION IS THE ONE THE RUBRIC ADMITS, on the RKD precedent: the fraud detector is an UPSTREAM filter on which cluster aggregates reach the unchanged inter-cluster aggregation, so removing it varies what arrives at a fixed downstream mechanism rather than deleting the downstream mechanism itself -- the opposite of the DROPlet and CrowdGuard-Table-V shape. A SECOND, INDEPENDENT ROUTE is §7.2.2's three-configuration inclusion contrast, "For each, we compare three configurations: (i) our protocol with inclusion under heterogeneous delays — 2 Gamma distributions for fast and slow clients, (ii) without inclusion under highly heterogeneous delays — fast clients are systematically over-represented, and (iii) without inclusion but with homogeneous delays — all clients draw from the same Gamma distribution, so no group is structurally favored;", read off the same downstream aggregation and reported as an outcome, "Without the inclusion mechanism, the aggregator converges to ≈ 50% accuracy on MNIST and ≈ 45% on CIFAR-5m — learning only half the label space.". Rule 4's benefit of the doubt is not needed for either arm. "ablation" has 0 hits; the paper never uses the word for either contrast, which is a seventh distinct C-d framing -- an arm presented as an appendix mechanism analysis

C-e.quote: Overall, we can see that the inclusion fraud detection mechanism is a necessary mechanism as it makes it possible to have a smoother training.
C-e.locator: §D.5; the claim names one constituent and says what it contributes to the composed result. The paper immediately supplies a MECHANISM-LEVEL EXPLANATION OF ITS OWN NULL, which is the more interesting half: "detection mechanism on the maximum accuracy of the training. This is probably due to the fact that, in the scenario without fraud detection, correct aggregators average the behaviour of the Byzantine behaviour, whose impact is therefore reduced." -- i.e. it attributes the absence of an effect on peak accuracy to averaging across correct aggregators diluting the Byzantine one. The hedge that sentence completes is "However, we cannot see a clear impact of the inclusion fraud[detection on the maximum accuracy of the training.]", split across a page boundary by the extractor (see the coder_note). A further constituent-level attribution is at §D.4, "As we can see, with 1, 2, or 3 crash, the crash of an aggregator does not impact the final accuracy of the correct aggregators."

papers.coder_note:
THE SCREENING NOTE PREDICTED THIS ROW AND GOT THE MECHANISM RIGHT AND THE OUTCOME WRONG, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE IT IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE SCREEN RATHER THAN ABOUT THE PAPER. The frozen screening reason reads: "borderline, included per the borderline rule: verifiable-coordinator clustering, LWE masking and differential privacy combined, though the threat is a Byzantine AGGREGATOR rather than a poisoning client, so C-c may well code NO". The threat is indeed a Byzantine aggregator and not a poisoning client -- the paper's clients are honest-but-curious and may only crash -- but C-c coded YES, because the paper does measure the assembled protocol's accuracy while an aggregator actively misbehaves. What the aggregator-not-client scope actually threatens is C-a, and that is where the row's real ambiguity sits.

THIS IS THE FRAME'S FIRST ROW WHERE AMENDMENT 3 EXCISES THE VERY CONSTITUENT THE PAPER'S ONLY PAIRING REASON REFERS TO, AND A5 MUST REPORT IT AS A THIRD LIMIT OF THE AMENDMENT. The paper does give a residual-coverage reason -- the fraud detector exists because the inclusion mechanism hands a Byzantine aggregator a new way to bias the model -- which is exactly the kind of sentence C-b was written to find. But the inclusion mechanism is fairness-purposed ("debiasing" client participation), so Amendment 3 removes it from C-a's count, and the surviving counted pair (PVAHSS verification, fraud detection) has no stated pairing reason at all. So the amendment can be sound at the level of each component and still destroy a criterion that quantifies relations BETWEEN components. The first limit was FedSAC's dual-purpose component; the second was DSFL-versus-GuardFed showing the test is not keyword-driven; this is the third, and it is the sharpest, because it changes a code rather than merely being hard to apply.

C-a = YES IS THE ROW'S ONE GENUINELY CONTESTABLE CODE AND I HAVE PUT EVERYTHING A READER NEEDS TO OVERTURN IT IN THE LOCATOR. The question is whether Amendment 3's "faulty, malicious or poisoned updates" reaches a Byzantine AGGREGATOR's wrong sum and biased cluster aggregate, or only a client's poisoned gradient. I read it as reaching them: both are inputs to the composition supplied by a participant deviating from the protocol, and the criterion's words are "faulty, malicious or poisoned", not "client". A reader who reads it the narrower way codes C-a = NO and the row leaves the DESIGN denominator entirely. NOTHING IN THE PRIMARY COUNT TURNS ON IT, because C-d = YES independently and on two separate arms, so the primary is NO under either reading. I therefore did NOT invoke ambiguity rule 1 to make the primary UNCLEAR: rule 1 exists to stop a coder guessing a primary, and here no guess is required -- ¬C-d is false on the paper's own figure. A5 should state that application of rule 1, because it is the first time a determined primary has coexisted with a contestable criterion, and because the alternative (UNCLEAR, hence excluded from numerator AND denominator) would have LOWERED the measured primary rate, i.e. moved it in the direction this paper's argument prefers.

C-d = YES ON TWO ARMS, NEITHER CALLED AN ABLATION, AND BOTH IN THE ADMITTED DIRECTION. Figure 15 turns the fraud detector off and on with the Byzantine behaviour fixed; §7.2.2 compares inclusion against no-inclusion against a homogeneous-delay upper-bound reference. In both, what varies is which client or cluster updates reach an unchanged aggregation, so the rubric's leave-one-out exclusion does not bite -- these are RKD-shaped, not DROPlet-shaped. The word "ablation" appears nowhere, and both contrasts live in an appendix section titled as a mechanism analysis; that is a SEVENTH distinct defeating framing for the C-d bucket, which surfaced neither arm.

A NEW EXTRACTION HAZARD, AND IT IS A THIRD KIND. The record's C-e hedge sentence is SPLIT ACROSS A PAGE BOUNDARY and the extractor placed the two halves ~2,700 characters apart in the WRONG ORDER: the opening clause is the last text in the file at offset 129377, and its continuation sits at 126605, immediately after a running head bearing the author list. The two halves are quoted separately here, and the tail half deliberately begins mid-word-boundary ("detection mechanism on the maximum accuracy...") rather than being silently rejoined. Column splicing (FedSAC) corrupts a sentence by interleaving a neighbour; layout interruption (GuardFed) breaks one with a macro artifact; THIS reorders a sentence's halves across thousands of characters, so a coder assembling a quotation by reading forward from the first half would find the sentence appears to end at "the inclusion fraud" and could easily complete it by hand -- the exact defect non-negotiable 5 forbids. THE DISTRIBUTIVE TEST, ARTICULATED AT ROW 47 AND NOT FROZEN IN ADVANCE, DECIDES C-a HERE. The paper makes two JOINT attributions -- the abstract's "coupling temporal smoothing with logits-only aggregation provides a communication-efficient and attack-resilient FL pipeline" and Table 1's "improved stability and robustness (via EMA and robust aggregation)" -- either of which, read as distributing over both constituents, would give the EMA stage a stated defense purpose and take C-a to YES on two components. Under FedSAC (2503.18284) I coded C-a = YES on exactly that grammar. The difference, and it is decisive, is that THIS paper elsewhere distributes the roles itself: "injecting temporal smoothing through server-side EMA and improving robustness via robust logit aggregation" assigns stability to the EMA and robustness to the aggregator, one clause each. FedSAC has no such sentence. So the rule is: when a paper attributes a conjunction of benefits to a conjunction of components, look for a sentence where it distributes them; if one exists, the distribution governs and the joint sentence is not a purpose statement for either component alone. Rule 3 points the same way, so this is not a rule-3 call -- it is the paper's own division of labour. A5 must report the distributive test alongside the granularity rule (row 45) as the second adjudication rule that Amendment 3's text does not settle, and must note that both were articulated mid-coding and are disclosed rather than retrofitted.

C-a = NO COSTS THE FRAME NOTHING AND THE PRIMARY IS NO UNDER EVERY READING. C-d = YES on Table 7 independently, so even a reader who takes the abstract's joint clause as EMA's purpose, codes C-a = YES and then also reaches C-b = YES lands at DESIGN = YES and primary = NO. Nothing in the totals moves on the distributive test except the DESIGN denominator's membership, and this row joins SRFed as the second row with C-a = NO and C-d = YES.

C-b IS THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF AMENDMENT 3'S EXCISED-CONSTITUENT LIMIT, AND IT CORRECTS THE GENERALIZATION THE THIRD INSTANCE DREW. The prior three are 2601.04930 (PPFA-BA: the residual-coverage reason refers to the inclusion mechanism, excised as fairness/debiasing), 2601.06466 (SecureDyn-FL: the Complementary Protection bullet pairs temporal gradient auditing with ENCRYPTION), and 2602.22269 (CQSA: the blinding-tension sentence pairs SECURE AGGREGATION with Byzantine detection).
